properties. A prominent peak is observed around 330 nm, indicating a strong absorption in this region, which 
is typical for many organic compounds. This peak suggests that Belzutifan has significant electronic transitions 
occurring at this wavelength, which could be attributed to π-π* transitions commonly associated with aromatic 
structures27. Beyond this peak, there is a gradual decline in absorption intensity towards longer wavelengths, 
with a secondary, less pronounced peak appearing around 450 nm. In addition to the main peak at 330 nm, the 
spectrum shows a broader and more subdued absorption feature extending from approximately 400 nm to 600 
nm. This behavior indicates that Belzutifan may have some degree of light absorption in the visible range, albeit 
weaker than in the ultraviolet range. The infrared (IR) spectrum of Belzutifan, illustrated in Fig. 2b, presents a 
complex pattern of absorption bands that provide valuable insights into the molecular structure and functional 
groups  present  in  the  compound.  The  spectrum  spans  a  range  from  approximately  4000  cm⁻¹  to  1000  cm⁻¹, 
with notable peaks that correspond to various vibrational modes of the molecular bonds. The presence of broad 
and intense absorption bands in the region around 3000–3500 cm⁻¹ typically indicates the presence of O-H or 
N-H stretching vibrations28. In the lower wavenumber region, particularly from 1500 cm⁻¹ to 1000 cm⁻¹, the 
spectrum reveals several sharp peaks that likely correspond to C = C stretching and C-H bending vibrations, 
common in aromatic compounds. The distinctive fingerprint region below 1500 cm⁻¹ can provide further details 
about the specific functional groups and bonding environments.

interactions. Simulations employed an NVT ensemble at 310 K (Langevin thermostat, γ = 1 ps⁻¹) to approximate 
physiological conditions, with a 1 fs time step verified by energy conservation tests and 5 ps duration sufficient 
for system equilibration as evidenced by RMSD plateauing after 2 ps. Trajectory analysis incorporated root mean 
square deviation (RMSD) calculations using backbone atoms, hydrogen bond identification (distance < 3.5 Å, 
angle > 150°), and charge transfer evaluation via Mulliken population analysis. Key assumptions include rigid 
nanocrystal surfaces and neutral pH conditions. Future work will incorporate surface defects and pH-dependent 
charge effects to better approximate biological environments.

SiC exhibits superior chemical stability in physiological environments (less than 5% degradation after 72 h in 
PBS16) and exceptional mechanical strength (Young’s modulus ≈ 440 GPa17). Recent studies have demonstrated 
SiC’s potential in drug delivery: PEGylated SiC nanoparticles showed 92% loading efficiency for paclitaxel with 
sustained release over 72 h18, while amino-functionalized SiC enhanced cellular uptake in MCF-7 cells by 2.3-
fold compared to non-functionalized particles19. Despite these advances, critical gaps remain in understanding 
SiC’s interactions with HIF inhibitors like Belzutifan. While molecular dynamics studies have examined SiC’s 
behavior with conventional chemotherapeutics20, no work has addressed its potential for targeted HIF inhibitor 
delivery.  Furthermore,  the  role  of  surface  functionalization  (-H,  -OH,  -COOH,  -NH₂)  in  modulating  drug-
nanocrystal  electronic  interactions  remains  unexplored—a  knowledge  gap  with  significant  implications  for 
controlled release systems. The application of SiC nanoparticles in drug delivery systems is further bolstered 
by their ability to facilitate controlled release. By modifying the surface properties of SiC, researchers can tailor 
the  release  kinetics  of  encapsulated  drugs21.  This  is  particularly  relevant  for  Belzutifan,  where  maintaining 
therapeutic concentrations above 50 ng/mL for > 12 h is crucial for HIF pathway suppression22. Moreover, SiC 
nanoparticles can be functionalized to enhance their interaction with specific biological targets23–25. Our work 
uniquely correlates electronic structure modifications with practical delivery metrics like adsorption stability 
and  optical  detection,  providing  a  roadmap  for  experimental  validation.  Computational  methods,  such  as 
density functional theory (DFT) and molecular dynamics (MD), have become invaluable tools in understanding 
drug-nanoparticle interactions at the molecular level. DFT allows for the exploration of electronic properties 
and binding affinities between Belzutifan and SiC nanoparticles, while MD simulations can provide insights into 
the dynamic behavior of these systems in biological environments. These computational studies can guide the 
design of more effective drug delivery systems.

This study employs density functional theory (DFT) and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to 
investigate silicon carbide (SiC) nanocrystals as carriers for the anticancer drug Belzutifan. Among 
tested functional groups (-H, -OH, -NH₂, -COOH), carboxyl-functionalized SiC (SiC-COOH) exhibits 
superior drug loading capacity with an adsorption energy of -1.03 eV, representing a 25% improvement 
over conventional carbon-based carriers. The SiC-COOH system demonstrates exceptional stability 
with a formation energy of -5.42 eV/atom and a remarkably high dipole moment of 142.1 D, facilitating 
enhanced solubility. Electronic structure analysis reveals significant charge transfers (-0.25e) from 
Belzutifan to the nanocrystal, accompanied by a substantial reduction in the HOMO-LUMO gap from 
5.427 eV (pristine SiC) to 3.41 eV (Belzutifan@SiC-COOH complex), indicating improved electronic 
coupling. MD simulations confirm the complex’s stability under physiological conditions, maintaining 
structural integrity with root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) values below 2.5 Å throughout the 5 
ps simulation. Characteristic shifts in optical spectra (200–600 nm range) and IR vibrational modes 
(15–40 cm⁻¹) provide clear spectroscopic signatures of successful drug adsorption. The combination 
of strong binding (-1.03 eV adsorption energy), maintained biocompatibility, and tunable electronic 
properties positions functionalized SiC nanocrystals as a promising platform for targeted Belzutifan 
delivery, with potential applications in photo-triggered release systems.

Conclusion
This computational study demonstrates that carboxyl-functionalized silicon carbide (SiC-COOH) nanocrystals 
exhibit  superior  performance  as  nanocarriers  for  Belzutifan  delivery,  achieving  a  high  adsorption  energy  of 
− 1.03 eV—25% stronger than conventional carbon-based carriers. The SiC-COOH system’s exceptional stability 
(formation energy: −5.42 eV/atom) and pronounced polarity (dipole moment: 142.1 D) facilitate both robust 
drug binding and enhanced solubility. Electronic structure analysis reveals critical charge transfers (− 0.25e) from 
Belzutifan to the nanocrystal, accompanied by a significant reduction in the HOMO-LUMO gap from 5.427 eV 
(pristine SiC) to 3.41 eV (Belzutifan@SiC-COOH), which enhances electronic coupling and suggests potential 
for photo-triggered release. Molecular dynamics simulations confirm the complex’s stability under physiological 
conditions, with structural deviations (RMSD) remaining below 2.5 Å over 5 ps, while spectroscopic shifts in 
the 200–600 nm range and IR vibrational changes (Δν = 15–40 cm⁻¹) provide detectable signatures of successful 
adsorption.  The  dominance  of  hydrogen  bonding  and  van  der  Waals  interactions,  as  evidenced  by  reduced 
density gradient analysis, underpins the system’s stability. These findings position SiC-COOH nanocrystals as 
a  promising  platform  for  targeted  Belzutifan  delivery,  addressing  key  challenges  in  solubility  and  controlled 
release for HIF inhibitor therapies. The insights gained from this work not only advance the design of ceramic-
based nanocarriers but also establish a computational framework for optimizing drug-nanoparticle interactions 
in oncology applications.

Computational details
The  computational  investigation  of  Belzutifan  adsorption  on  silicon  carbide  (SiC)  nanoparticles  integrated 
density  functional  theory  (DFT)  and  molecular  dynamics  (MD)  simulations  to  elucidate  both  electronic 
and  dynamic  interactions.  DFT  calculations  were  performed  using  the  OpenMX  package23,  which  employs 
optimized  pseudopotentials  and  localized  basis  sets  for  efficient  large-scale  simulations  of  hybrid  organic-
inorganic  systems.  The  PBE-D3  exchange-correlation  functional24–27  was  selected  for  its  validated  accuracy 
in  modeling  drug-nanomaterial  interactions,  combining  the  generalized  gradient  approximation  (PBE)  with 
Grimme’s D3 dispersion correction28 including Becke-Johnson damping29. This approach is particularly suited 
for physisorption studies, as it accurately captures van der Waals forces that dominate drug-surface binding, with 
benchmark studies demonstrating mean absolute errors < 0.1 eV for adsorption energies of organic molecules 
on  semiconductors30.  The  LCPAO-s2p2d2  basis  set25,31  was  chosen  for  its  optimized  radial  functions  that 
provide superior convergence for SiC systems compared to standard Gaussian-type orbitals, while maintaining 
computational efficiency – tests show < 0.01 Å differences in bond lengths versus larger s3p3d3 sets for similar 
systems32. To model the nanoparticle environment, a hexagonal 4 H-SiC unit cell (64 atoms) was constructed 
with lattice parameters (a = 3.073 Å, c = 10.053 Å) matching experimental crystallographic data33, and surface 
termination  followed  the  most  stable  (110)  orientation  as  determined  by  previous  DFT-MD  studies33,34. The

Conclusion
This computational study demonstrates that carboxyl-functionalized silicon carbide (SiC-COOH) nanocrystals 
exhibit  superior  performance  as  nanocarriers  for  Belzutifan  delivery,  achieving  a  high  adsorption  energy  of 
− 1.03 eV—25% stronger than conventional carbon-based carriers. The SiC-COOH system’s exceptional stability 
(formation energy: −5.42 eV/atom) and pronounced polarity (dipole moment: 142.1 D) facilitate both robust 
drug binding and enhanced solubility. Electronic structure analysis reveals critical charge transfers (− 0.25e) from 
Belzutifan to the nanocrystal, accompanied by a significant reduction in the HOMO-LUMO gap from 5.427 eV 
(pristine SiC) to 3.41 eV (Belzutifan@SiC-COOH), which enhances electronic coupling and suggests potential 
for photo-triggered release. Molecular dynamics simulations confirm the complex’s stability under physiological 
conditions, with structural deviations (RMSD) remaining below 2.5 Å over 5 ps, while spectroscopic shifts in 
the 200–600 nm range and IR vibrational changes (Δν = 15–40 cm⁻¹) provide detectable signatures of successful 
adsorption.  The  dominance  of  hydrogen  bonding  and  van  der  Waals  interactions,  as  evidenced  by  reduced 
density gradient analysis, underpins the system’s stability. These findings position SiC-COOH nanocrystals as 
a  promising  platform  for  targeted  Belzutifan  delivery,  addressing  key  challenges  in  solubility  and  controlled 
release for HIF inhibitor therapies. The insights gained from this work not only advance the design of ceramic-
based nanocarriers but also establish a computational framework for optimizing drug-nanoparticle interactions 
in oncology applications.
